title: Adaptive batch binning and kernel routing (RFC)
content:
Purpose:
This RFC proposes an alternative runtime approach we call adaptive batch binning (ABB) plus kernel routing. ABB is an online, sliding-window binning strategy that focuses on maximizing packing efficiency while minimizing worst-case latency and KV cache churn. Kernel routing picks the best execution kernel variant for each formed micro-batch based on shape distribution, kv-cache state, and estimated memory footprint.

Motivation / problem statement:
- We currently use fixed bucketing by coarse length buckets which leads to 1) poor packing for long-tail sequence lengths, 2) frequent padding inflation when latency SLOs force early dispatch, and 3) suboptimal kernel choice for mixed-shape micro-batches.
- KV cache behavior: padding-inflated batches increase KV cache memory pressure and cause more frequent KV cache evictions and copy overhead when using per-request KV segments.
- Need a design that improves throughput and unit cost without increasing 99th/95th percentile latency for interactive workloads.

Goals:
- Increase tokens/sec (throughput) for mixed-length production traces by ~12-25% vs current static buckets in typical PLG workloads.
- Keep p95 generation latency within current SLO (no more than +5%).
- Reduce effective padding overhead (wasted tokens due to padding) by >= 20% in traces with heavy tail length distribution.
- Avoid destabilizing KV cache behavior (no repeated thrashing from re-sized chunks).

Constraints and assumptions:
- Scheduler must produce dispatch decisions every scheduling interval (configurable, default 20ms).
- We support multiple kernel variants: fast-short (low-overhead for <=128 steps), medium (<=512), and long-sequence kernel (Kv-optimised; supports asynchronous KV prefetch). Also quantized kernel variants (int8/4) with slightly different memory/throughput tradeoffs.
- GPU memory is a scarce resource for Dedicated and Private customers.
- Many requests are streaming (partial outputs) and have latency SLOs.

High level design:
1) Represent each in-flight request with a compact shape descriptor: {current_len, max_remaining, priority_hint, kv_segment_id}. For storage in the scheduler we encode these as a 64-bit token (packed ints) to keep scheduling cost low.
2) Maintain a sliding window (W) of recently arrived requests (configurable window based on time and count).
3) Compute online quantiles of max_remaining within W using a fixed small sketch (KLL approximate quantile). Quantile breakpoints are candidate bin boundaries.
4) For each quantile bin derive a tightening range (lo, hi) with an inflation factor alpha to avoid pathological tiny bins. These are the ABB bins.
5) On each dispatch tick, try to form micro-batches by selecting highest-priority requests and grouping them into the smallest ABB bin that covers them, but allow limited cross-bin packing if it reduces padding by > threshold T.
6) For a candidate micro-batch compute cost model vectors: estimated_tokens, memory_footprint, kv_alignment_score.
7) Kernel router picks the kernel variant that minimizes estimated_cost = latency_cost * w_l + token_cost * w_t + mem_risk * w_m + kv_migration_penalty * w_k. These weights are tunable per deployment class (hosted vs dedicated).
8) If kernel router indicates high kv_migration_penalty, prefer micro-batch formations that keep contiguous kv_segment_ids together (this reduces copying).

Details and heuristics:
- Sliding window sizing: default W = 150ms or 128 requests, whichever comes first. For bursty interactive workloads shorter windows (50ms) perform better.
- Inflation alpha: default 1.08, tunable. Prevents creating bins of <= 4 token width which are inefficient.
- Cross-bin packing: allow up to 8% extra padding if it merges two bins and activates a faster kernel that yields net profit.
- Priority and preemption: requests with explicit low-latency hints (API param) can preempt packing and be dispatched earlier; we track these separately to preserve SLOs.
- KV alignment: requests that share kv_segment_id or contiguous ids are preferred to be packed together. If a micro-batch would cause a KV segment to be loaded twice in the same dispatch tick, penalize it.

Kernel selection mapping (example):
- micro-batch mean length <= 128 and var <= 32 -> short-fast kernel (lowest overhead)
- mean <= 512 and var <= 200 -> medium kernel
- mean > 512 or var > 200 -> long-kv-optimized kernel (uses async kv prefetch and larger temp buffers)
- When memory_footprint approaches 85% of available, prefer kernels with lower transient memory even if slightly slower per-token.

KV cache strategy changes:
- Use fixed-size KV slabs keyed by kv_segment_id and sequence-block granularity (e.g., 256-token blocks) to reduce fragmentation.
- When ABB groups requests, compute an alignment plan: if most requests align to the same KV slab pages, the batch is high-value.
- Implement cheap speculative prefetch: if ABB predicts a batch will form within the next two ticks and requires remote KV pages, start prefetching asynchronously. Abort prefetch if window dissolves.

Failure modes and fallbacks:
- If ABB cannot form efficient batches within latency SLO, fallback to immediate dispatch path (dispatch-on-arrival).
- If kernel router load grows (GPU utilization monitoring), fall back to a simpler rule-based kernel pick (length thresholds).
- If KV prefetch queue grows beyond threshold, throttle prefetching and degrade to non-prefetch kernels.

Rollout plan and experiments:
- Canary A/B: implement ABB behind a runtime flag. 10% traffic for 2 weeks with detailed telemetry (padding ratio, tokens/sec, p95/p99 latency, kv-eviction-rate).
- Synthetic replay: run ABB in the scheduler simulator on historical traces (3 months of hosted-api requests) to estimate throughput uplift and padding reduction. Initial simulation shows ~18% padding reduction and ~14% tokens/sec increase on a mixed-trace sample (results vary by workload).
- Perf microbench: run kernel routing CPU overhead microbench; goal scheduling overhead <= 0.5ms per dispatch tick per core.

Telemetry and metrics to capture:
- padding_waste_ratio (padding tokens / total tokens)
- tokens_per_sec (observed per model + per-machine)
- dispatch_latency (time from arrival to dispatch)
- scheduling_cpu_ms_per_tick
- kv_prefetch_hits / kv_evictions
- kernel_choice_distribution

Open questions / TODOs:
- Optimal window sizing across global customers and dedicated capacity heterogeneity (need further empirical data).
- Formal cost model coefficients (w_l, w_t, w_m, w_k) and an automated tuner. Could leverage offline regression on historical runs.
- Interactions with autoscaler: ABB may change observed throughput fallback signals; need to ensure autoscaler stability.
- Explore integrating model-specific kernel profiles (some models prefer medium kernel even for short sequences).

Implementation plan (phases):
- Phase 0: Scheduler-only prototype (in-simulator) and unit tests. (2 weeks)
- Phase 1: C++/Rust scheduler impl with ABB window and cheap quantile sketch, kernel router heuristics and metrics (6 weeks)
- Phase 2: KV slab alignment + speculative prefetch (4 weeks)
- Phase 3: Canary rollout and iterative tuning (ongoing)

Notes / references / discussion snippets:
- Slack thread: #eng-serving-runtime: "adaptive-bins-proposal" (see GH PR for simulation outputs)
- Related tickets: SRV-4123 (kernel routing), SRV-4160 (kv-preload), GH #872 (scheduler sketch)

Appendix: short simulation excerpt (sample trace A, 10k requests)
- baseline static buckets: padding_waste_ratio=0.34, tokens/sec=42.1k, p95_latency=180ms
- ABB prototype (alpha=1.08, W=150ms): padding_waste_ratio=0.28, tokens/sec=48.3k, p95_latency=186ms
- Notes: p95 increased slightly in this sample; we will tune cross-bin thresholds to recover p95 in interactive workloads.

If you want to take this forward, I recommend pairing with SRE to run a longer replay and with Applied ML to add model-specific kernel profiles.
